newsitem.title: USA: Maine utility deregulation plan released.
newsitem.headline: Maine utility deregulation plan released.

text.p: Maine's electric utility industry would be deregulated into a competive market by Jan. 2000 under a proposal released Tuesday by the Public Utilities, Commission.

Regulators want investor-owned utilities to seperate their generation assets from their distribution businesses by 2000 - with the two largest companies, Central Maine Power and Bangor Hydro, required to divest generation assets by 2006.
The proposal was requested by Legislature, which is scheduled to debate regulation legislation in 1997.
The regulators said customers should be allowed to form aggregate purchasing groups and buy either directly from power suppliers or from intermediaries such as energy service companies.

The PUC said deregulation "should create significant benefits to Maine and its consumers" but the report did not specifically estimate how much money the changeover would save consumers or cost existing utilities.

The report recommends utilities have a "reasonable opportunity" to recover costs "stranded" by a shift to a competitive market with such costs collected by the newly created transmission and distribution companies.
The PUC said it will develop an initial estimate on the extent of stranded costs before 2000 and that it would only involve investments made by utilities prior to March 1995.

The regulators said Maine Public Service - which is nearly entirely dependent on Canadian-produced power - should not be required to divest its generating assets but would be restricted to retailing in its current service area.
Maine's consumer-owned utilities would be restricted after 2005 to marketing power within their service territories, the report recommends.

The commissioners recommended that Maine consumers be allowed to buy power from producers in other states and Canadian provinces even if the jurisdictions do not allow retail competition in their own area.

An opinion survey conducted in drafting Tuesday's proposal found Maine consumers are leary of efforts to deregulate the electric industry and many would be willing to pay more if there were environmental benefits.

The survey released in late November found only 41 percent of residential users and 50 percent of small business consumers favored deregulation while 54.5 of the residential and 47.3 of the businesses opposed the idea.
